newsitem.title: GREECE: NZ SPORT-FAUMUINA SUCCESS MAKES UP FOR NZ FLOPS.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT-FAUMUINA SUCCESS MAKES UP FOR NZ FLOPS.

text.p: ATHENS, Aug 11 - Athens '97 will always be remembered as the meet where New Zealand won its first world athletics championship gold medal.
But Beatrice Faumuina's success in the women's discus was one extreme for a team whose performances varied from the outstanding to the outrageous.
Faumuina, 800m runner Toni Hodgkinson and road walker Craig Barrett fall into the former category.

The latter encompasses most of New Zealand's middle distance runners, notably 5000m pair Anne Hare and Jonathan Wyatt, javelin thrower Gavin Lovegrove and decathlete Douglas Pirini who knocked himself out -- almost literally -- by jumping into a high jump support.

Athletics New Zealand changed its selection policy in the wake of the Atlanta Olympics debacle, but too many New Zealand athletes are still turning out less than their best performances at world level when everything is now being done to ensure only healthy athletes in peak form are picked.
Six of the New Zealand athletes could be classed as failures, against five successes and a further six who did enough to justify their selection.
Of those failures, only distance runner Nyla Carroll and walker Scott Nelson were injury-affected, with Nelson's affecting him for the first time during the race itself.

The worst cases were Hare and Wyatt, who both ran off the track before the end of their respective 5000m heats. Hare claimed she had trouble breathing; Wyatt didn't even offer an excuse, simply saying: "I just lost it".

Pirini was the architect of his own demise, gashing his head on a high jump support, while the highly-rated Lovegrove added to his catalogue of failures by falling at the first phase for the fourth major championship in succession.
The failures are a continual source of anguish to New Zealand team manager Dave Norris, who had billed this team as the biggest and "best-prepared" to be sent to any major championship.
"A third of the team were disappointments, and to be fair they are disappointed themselves," Norris, who also heads New Zealand's selection panel, said.
"At Atlanta we had roughly half the team that were injured or out of form, so we changed our selection policy to be able to remove people who weren't up to scratch after they had qualified.
"This time we have had two injured -- and one who injured himself (Pirini) -- and three out of form.
"We thought everyone who had come into camp had been monitored closely and was in form and injury free.
"The best I can say is that at least we are getting in place a system to ensure that people are physically prepared.
"Mental preparation is much harder and usually only comes with experience.
"Perhaps sports science or psychology can help overcome the mental pressures, which you really only experience at these big events."

Inexperience wouldn't account for the performances of Lovegrove, a double Commonwealth bronze medallist and veteran of four world championships and two Olympics, or Hare, the 33-year-old team captain whose international career also began at the 1986 Commonwealth Games.
Norris said he and team coaches held discussions with athletes to go over their performances, particularly in the light of failure.
"There is a follow-up process where we have discussions with the athlete to find out what the story was," he added.
"In some cases like Nyla and Scott it was physical distress, which was a surprise to us and them.
"Anne and Jonathan did PBs (personal bests) in the last fortnight, so it appeared their form was good.
"They have to analyse their training to find out why on the day their bodies just turned to jelly.
"And Gavin...Well, he is just an enigma."

Nelson has returned home for treatment on his injury, thought to be a strained shoulder muscle which affects his race walking action, while the New Zealand team has been unsuccessful in attempts to obtain a bone scan for Carroll's injured foot.
She is likely to have treatment when she returns home with the team next week.
